name: Azariah
title: King of Judah, also known as Uzziah
summary: Azariah, better known by the name Uzziah, ascended Judah's throne at sixteen and reigned for 52 years—one of the longest reigns in Judah's history. Under his leadership, the kingdom experienced remarkable prosperity: he defeated the Philistines and other neighboring peoples, fortified Jerusalem with powerful towers, organized a mighty army, and invested in agricultural development in the desert regions. He sought God under the guidance of the prophet Zechariah, and as long as he did so, God gave him success. But when pride took hold of his heart, he overstepped the divinely appointed order by entering the temple to burn incense himself—a holy service reserved for the descendants of Aaron. The priests confronted him, but the king flew into a rage. Immediately, leprosy broke out on his forehead, and he had to live the rest of his life in isolation while his son Jotham served as regent. It was in the year Uzziah died that the prophet Isaiah received his powerful calling through a vision of the Lord seated on His throne in the temple—an event that forms a striking theological contrast to the fallen king's arrogance.

keyEvents.title: Azariah becomes king over Judah
keyEvents.description: Azariah became king at the age of sixteen, following the death of his father Amaziah, and reigned for 52 years in Jerusalem.

keyEvents.title: Azariah does what is right in the Lord's eyes
keyEvents.description: He did what was right in the Lord's eyes, just as his father Amaziah had done, and sought God under the guidance of Zechariah.

keyEvents.title: Great military and economic expansion
keyEvents.description: Uzziah built up a strong army, fortified Jerusalem with towers, waged war against the Philistines and other nations, and promoted agriculture with irrigation systems. He became powerful, and his fame spread far and wide.

keyEvents.title: Azariah struck with leprosy after sacrilege
keyEvents.description: In his pride, Azariah entered the Lord's temple to burn incense on the altar of incense, which was reserved for the priests. Priest Azariah and eighty other priests tried to stop him, but the king became furious. Then leprosy broke out on his forehead while he stood before the priests at the altar of incense.

keyEvents.title: Jotham rules as regent
keyEvents.description: Because Azariah had leprosy, he lived in a separate house isolated from others, and his son Jotham took charge of the king's household and judged the people in the land.

keyEvents.title: Isaiah's prophetic call at Uzziah's death
keyEvents.description: The prophet Isaiah received his calling in the year King Uzziah died, when he saw the Lord sitting on a high and exalted throne in the temple. This vision marks a turning point in Judah's prophetic history.

He did what was right in the Lord's eyes and led Judah to great military and economic progress, but was struck with leprosy after entering the temple to burn incense, which was reserved for the priests.

footnotes.text: The name Azariah (Hebrew עֲזַרְיָה, 'Azarjah') means 'the Lord has helped', while Uzziah (עֻזִּיָּהוּ, 'Uzzijjahu') means 'the Lord is my strength'. It is unclear why the king had two names. In 2 Kings the name Azariah is used primarily, while 2 Chronicles consistently uses Uzziah. Some scholars believe one was a throne name and the other a personal name.

A limestone tablet from the 1st century CE, known as the 'Uzziah Tombstone', was found on the Mount of Olives in Jerusalem and bears an Aramaic inscription that reads: 'Here were brought the bones of Uzziah, king of Judah. Do not open.' This inscription testifies that his remains were moved at a later time, possibly due to his leprosy status, which rendered his original burial site ritually unclean.

Azariah's attempt to burn incense in the temple represents a serious violation of the biblical order in which royal and priestly authority were separated. In ancient Israel, only the Levitical priesthood had the right to serve at the altar (Num 18:1–7). This event underscores the biblical principle that even kings stood under God's law and could not presume to act arbitrarily in worship.

According to 2 Chr 26:6–15, Uzziah's reign was marked by significant military and economic expansion. He waged war against the Philistines, built fortifications, and developed agriculture with irrigation systems in the Negev. Archaeological excavations in the Negev region have uncovered fortifications and agricultural installations that some scholars date to his period, which may support the Chronicler's account of his building activities.

The prophet Isaiah received his call 'in the year King Uzziah died' (Isa 6:1). Thus, Uzziah's death marks a turning point in Judah's history, and Isaiah's vision of the Lord's glory in the temple—the same temple where Uzziah had sinned—creates a strong theological contrast between the earthly king's pride and the heavenly King's holiness.

The Assyrian king Tiglath-Pileser III mentions in his annals a coalition of Syrian and Palestinian kings, and some scholars have identified 'Azriau of Yaudi' in these texts with Azariah/Uzziah of Judah, although this identification is disputed. If the connection is correct, it testifies that Azariah's power extended far enough to make him an actor in the regional resistance against Assyria.

Rabbinic tradition (Talmud Bavli, Sotah 10a) links Uzziah's leprosy to pride and draws parallels with other biblical figures who were struck down for overstepping their bounds. Midrash literature expands on the earthquake mentioned in Amos 1:1 and Zech 14:5, connecting it directly to the moment Uzziah entered the temple—as if creation itself reacted to his sacrilege.
